title: Babies' and children's hair
question_forms: How do I look after a Black baby's or toddler's hair?
Are braids and tight styles safe for children's hair?
tradition_says: Babies' hair is oiled and greased early, braided and sealed, and tight styles are used to keep it neat for school. Some believe a baby's early hair must be cut or oiled to grow thick.

layer1.plain_answer: Children's hair is best handled the way adults' is: gently, with hair wet and conditioned for detangling. Tight braids and updos are linked to traction alopecia in Black girls; larger braids, fewer extensions and looser styles are advised. Cradle cap is harmless. My search found nothing aimed at adoptive parents, but the same guidance applies.

do.text: Detangle only when hair is wet and conditioned.

source.name: Dermatology Times, report of a talk by B Kenner-Bell MD (paediatric dermatologist), Society for Pediatric Dermatology 2026, "Teaching kids to love their hair"

do.text: Choose larger braids or locs, fewer extensions, and loosen tight styles.

source.name: Dermatology Times, report of a talk by B Kenner-Bell MD (paediatric dermatologist), Society for Pediatric Dermatology 2026, "Teaching kids to love their hair"

do.text: Remove extensions at least monthly and allow 4 to 6 weeks of recovery between long styles.

source.name: Dermatology Times, report of a talk by B Kenner-Bell MD (paediatric dermatologist), Society for Pediatric Dermatology 2026, "Teaching kids to love their hair"

do.text: For cradle cap, massage in emollient or coconut oil, brush gently, then wash with baby shampoo.

source.name: Dermatology Times, report of a talk by B Kenner-Bell MD (paediatric dermatologist), Society for Pediatric Dermatology 2026, "Teaching kids to love their hair"

avoid.text: Tight braids and cornrows: in one caregiver survey cornrows were associated with traction alopecia among girls from non-dermatology clinics only, not the dermatology clinic group.
Olive oil, peanut oil, soap, adult shampoos or fragranced products on cradle cap.
Picking cradle cap crusts: it can raise the risk of infection.

see_someone_when: Thinning, bald patches or a sore scalp from a hairstyle (doctor or paediatrician).
Cradle cap that does not improve after a few weeks, or covers the whole body (doctor).
Crusts that bleed or leak fluid, or swollen areas (doctor).

tested.population: 574 African schoolgirls (6-21 years) and 604 women (18-86 years), South Africa
tested.design: Two population studies analysed together; logistic regression
tested.finding: Traction alopecia was present in 17.1% of schoolgirls and 31.7% of women. Risk was highest when traction was added to relaxed hair (odds ratio 3.47 against natural hair, 95% CI 1.94-6.20).

source.authors: Khumalo NP, Jessop S, Gumedze F, Ehrlich R
source.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology

tested.population: 201 caregivers of African American girls aged 1-15, US clinics
tested.finding: Cornrows were associated with traction alopecia in the non-dermatology clinic group (adjusted odds ratio 5.79, 95% CI 1.35-24.8). For seborrhoeic dermatitis, extensions (odds ratio 2.37) and infrequent oil use (3.69) were associated; wash frequency was not. 99% used oils or grease, 80% hot combs, 42% chemical relaxers.

source.authors: Rucker Wright D, Gathers R, Kapke A, Johnson D et al
source.journal: Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology

tested.note: Caregiver report, small, wide confidence intervals; associations only.

tested.population: 310 children aged 0 to 24 months, six trials
tested.design: Cochrane review of treatments for infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis (cradle cap)
tested.finding: Six trials compared oral biotin against placebo, proprietary products against placebo or control shampoo, and topical steroids against other products; the trials were short (10 to 42 days) and the results were based on very low-quality evidence.

source.authors: Victoire A, Magin P et al

tested.note: Trials not in Black children specifically.

tested.design: PubMed search 12 Nov 2026: (hair care) AND (adoptive OR adopted OR transracial) AND (Black OR African American) AND (children OR child); 0 hits. Positive control: (traction alopecia) AND (children) returned 55 hits.
tested.finding: My search found nothing: nothing from a clinical source; the guidance here comes from paediatric dermatology and the NHS for any parent.

tier_driver: That tight styles are associated with traction alopecia in African and African American girls: cross-sectional and caregiver studies.
tier_note: Observational; the paediatric dermatology advice comes from a conference talk reported in trade press, not a trial. Cradle cap treatments are very low-quality evidence.
harm_note: Traction alopecia in 17% of schoolgirls in one South African sample (Khumalo 2008); caregiver report links cornrows to it (Rucker Wright 2011).
evidence_summary: In 574 South African schoolgirls, 17.1% had traction alopecia (Khumalo 2008). Caregivers of African American girls reported cornrows associated with it (odds ratio 5.79) and 99% used oils or grease, 80% hot combs and 42% relaxers (Rucker Wright 2011). A paediatric dermatologist (reported by Dermatology Times, 2026) advises larger braids, fewer extensions, monthly extension removal and 4 to 6 weeks of rest. The Cochrane review of cradle cap treatments found six short trials with very low-quality evidence (Victoire 2019). The NHS says cradle cap is harmless and clears in a few months. The BAD leaflet notes traction alopecia is often seen in women and children of African descent.
gaps: Rucker Wright 2011: the cornrow link held in non-dermatology clinic respondents only (aOR 5.79, 1.35 to 24.8); the plain answer rests on Khumalo 2008 for tight styles in general. Untested: any baby or toddler hair routine in a trial; safe age for first braiding; whether baby hair texture changes (no source). Nothing found aimed at adoptive parents.
